new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Direct physical contacts with epithelial cells regulate leukocyte actin dynamics to facilitate intraepithelial motility in vivo
new_this_week.abstract: Efficient immune cell migration requires physical interactions with surrounding tissues. While tissue matrix mechanics influence leukocyte motility, it is unknown how leukocytes exert pushing and pulling forces to traverse cell-dense epithelial tissues in vivo. Here, we leverage the optical transparency of larval zebrafish to identify how physical interactions with epithelial cells regulate mechanisms of neutrophil force generation to navigate cell-dense tissues. Confining forces from epithelial cells induce a mechanosensitive central actin network, mediated by Cdc42 and Wiskott–Aldrich Syndrome Protein, which exerts expansile forces on surrounding cells to dilate a path for migration. In concert, direct cell-to-cell (leukocyte–epithelial) contacts mediated by integrin ɑE recognition of epithelial cadherin generate traction forces to enable forward motility. Together, our findings identify how physical interactions with the surrounding cellular environment regulate leukocyte motility through epithelial tissue in vivo.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Discovery and characterization of miranthins, “Trojan horse” antibiotic modulators of bacterial composition in the oral microbiome
new_this_week.abstract: Bacteria of the human microbiota encode an abundance of natural products that likely mediate bacterial competition, local colonization patterns, and human health and disease. However, very few of these compounds have been identified and characterized to date. During our investigation of Streptococcus mitis , an important early colonizer of the oral cavity, we identified and structurally characterized a family of peptide natural products, termed miranthins herein, that contain an unusual macrocycle formed by an Asp-Cys β-carbon thioether crosslink. We determined that the most abundantly secreted miranthin is a “Trojan horse” antibiotic that enters sensitive cells via the Ami oligopeptide transporter, is hydrolyzed and activated by aminopeptidase N, and subsequently inhibits ribosomal translation to curb the growth of streptococcal competitors. The miranthins are narrow-spectrum antibiotics that could enable S. mitis to modulate community dynamics in the oral cavity, highlighting the importance of peptide natural products in interspecies competition in the microbiome.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization
new_this_week.abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions—abrupt or gradual—and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Field experiments predict ecological response to a large-scale epidemic of an anti-keystone pathogen
new_this_week.abstract: Knowledge of how pathogens, in the context of a changing environment, shape the structure of ecological communities remains limited, and little information exists on the ability of small-scale field experiments to predict the consequences of large-scale environmental impacts. We addressed these issues using the emergence of a widespread epidemic (sea star wasting disease, SSWD) on rocky intertidal shorelines. Prior experiments demonstrated strong reductions in sessile species diversity in response to the local experimental removal of the sea star Pisaster ochraceus [R. T. Paine, Am. Nat. 100 , 65–75 (1966); R. T. Paine, Oceologia 15 , 93–120 (1974)] at our site. In surveys of sea star populations over 8 y spanning the onset of the SSWD epidemic, P. ochraceus populations declined by 90%, then subsequently recovered to about one third of pre-epidemic size under an endemic disease phase. Using four different types of temporal data, we documented large increases in populations of the competitively dominant mussel Mytilus californianus following P. ochraceus decline, which were of similar magnitude to those observed in prior field experiments. As in the field experiments, sessile species richness and diversity declined strongly following the onset of the SSWD epidemic as mussels were released from predator control. Our results reveal a strong effect of a pathogen in regulating ecological community structure by disrupting the role of a keystone species, a result anticipated by prior small-scale field experiments.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: In mice, a population of male germ cells shows characteristics of nonapoptotic cell death during G0 arrest
new_this_week.abstract: In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for the male’s reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells (MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In this study, we used a mouse model to characterize a population of MGCs that begin to accumulate markers of cell death, such as AnnexinV (AnV) and propidium iodide (PI), at E16.5. The AnV- and PI-positive MGC population is characterized by low expression of the RNA-binding protein, Dead End 1, and exhibits dsDNA breaks and mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, we do not see evidence of an active cell death cascade until the time of birth, when phosphorylation of MLKL, a hallmark of necroptotic cell death, occurs. Based on these findings, we propose that variable cellular health is an important basis for selection of SSC precursors.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
new_this_week.abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector
new_this_week.abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
new_this_week.abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
new_this_week.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH 4 -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT
new_this_week.abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin , which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3′ untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

new_this_week.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
new_this_week.title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
new_this_week.abstract: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) has been observed across virtually all tropospheric environments, yet the meteorological conditions that favor or suppress it have resisted clear theoretical resolution. Here we show that, for neutral chemistries in which a strongly bound molecular pair constitutes the critical cluster, the thermodynamic precondition for NPF is set by a single quantity: the effective binding free energy of that pair, Δ G AB ° ( T , RH ) , which captures the competing influences of temperature and relative humidity in a closed-form analytical framework. Applied to the sulfuric acid–dimethylamine system in the boundary layer, the theory reproduces observed clustering across laboratory experiments and field campaigns spanning a polluted megacity, a remote high-altitude site, and an ultra-pristine boreal peatland, all without kinetic fitting parameters; precursor concentrations and the condensation sink enter as separable factors that govern the subsequent production rate. The framework reveals an optimal Δ G AB ° that maximizes cluster production, providing a thermodynamic basis for why NPF peaks at midday, favors spring over other seasons, occurs under heat wave conditions despite temperatures approaching + 40 ° C, and can even arise on rare evenings in near-pristine conditions. More broadly, the theory exposes the inherent relationship between atmospheric conditions and the earliest steps of particle formation, offering a general interpretive tool that complements and extends what observations and simulations alone cannot provide.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Human Imagery and Psychological Reactance in Persuasive Health Messages
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Although mass-mediated persuasive messages often feature images of people, their impacts are surprisingly understudied. We tested whether attributes of human imagery influence psychological reactance to a health promotion PSA, either alone or combined with language style. Participants ( N = 1,100) viewed a message promoting sun safety that contained a forceful (vs. courteous) appeal and featured a model with forceful (vs. neutral) body language. The model’s physical characteristics (gender and skin tone) also varied. Both forceful text and forceful body language indirectly lowered protective behavioral intentions via reactance, and male-model messages had this effect for female participants. Our findings demonstrate the potential for features of human imagery to inadvertently hinder persuasion. Study results also highlight the value in measuring perceived visual freedom threat alongside traditional reactance measures. We discuss implications for reactance theory and measurement and highlight important directions for research on reactance to visuals.

previous_week_catch_up.title: HCV incidence and prevalence trends among people who use drugs in France 2004 to 2023
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a key public health challenge, particularly among people who use and inject drugs (PWUD, PWID). While direct-acting antivirals (DAA) have revolutionized HCV treatment, meeting the WHO’s 2030 elimination target requires accurate estimation of incidence and prevalence to guide prevention and care. We analyze cross-sectional surveys conducted in France in 2004, 2013, and 2023, recruiting PWUD at harm reduction services and collecting behavioral and biological data. We estimate age-and time-dependent prevalence of HCV antibodies and HCV RNA using multivariate regression models while incidence was estimated from two-state transmission models. The demographic profile of PWUD has aged over time (mean age 35 years in 2004 vs. 44 in 2023) while injection prevalence remained stable (61.7% in 2023). Between 2013 and 2023, HCV burden declined substantially: HCV RNA prevalence fell from 19.4% (95% CI 16.3–23.0) to 9.5% (7.2–12.3) among all PWUD, and from 29.6% to 14.5% among PWID. Incidence among PWID decreased from 6.5 (4.1–8.0) to 2.4 (1.4–4.2) per 100 person-years. These reductions likely reflect the combined impact of DAA scale-up and harm reduction policies, marking substantial progress toward elimination targets. However, ongoing transmission highlights persistent barriers requiring targeted public health actions.

previous_week_catch_up.title: In situ reduction-driven formation of sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures provide a platform for modulating electronic structure and interfacial reactivity through strong atom-level coupling, with potential applications in energy conversion. However, their precise construction remains challenging. Here we show a strategy for constructing sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures through confined spinodal decomposition and ligand-mediated in situ reduction. Oleylamine ligands adsorbed on NiMoO4 sub-nanowires act as mild reductants, selectively reducing Ni2+ to spatially confined metallic Ni domains and forming coherent Ni/NiMoO4 heterointerfaces. Experimental and theoretical analyses suggest that the Ni/NiMoO4 interfaces modify the local electronic structure and facilitate the adsorption and activation of hydrogen evolution intermediates. The resulting catalyst requires an overpotential of 14.4 ± 2.9 mV to reach 10 mA cm−2 in 1 M KOH and delivers 2 A cm−2 at 1.62 V in an anion-exchange membrane electrolyzer at 80 oC, with stable operation over 2200 h at 25 °C. These findings provide insights into the construction and interfacial regulation of sub-nanometer heterostructures through in situ reduction. Sub-nanometer heterostructures offer opportunities to tune interfacial reactivity, but their precise construction remains challenging. Here, the authors report alternating Ni/NiMoO₄ heterostructures that promote hydrogen evolution and sustain durable high-current electrolysis.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Who Verifies the Verifiers? AI, Local Knowledge Production, and Credibility in Tanzania’s 2025 Election
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: This study examines how Factchecking AI tools and community-based credibility practices interacted during Tanzania’s 2025 presidential election. Using data from five regions, we analyzed 342 media materials, 87 interviews, field observations, and 22 distinct contested election events. The findings identify three forms of verification disjuncture. First, AI-assisted translation and transcription sometimes changed the meaning of politically important statements before journalists could verify them. Second, fact-checks and disputed claims often moved through different communication channels, which limited the chances that people would see the correction. Third, some communities trusted personal experience, familiar sources, and collective discussion more than professional fact-checkers. Participants judged credibility through relationships, lived experience, group discussion, humor and satire, and social accountability. These practices sometimes supported the same conclusions as institutional verification and sometimes produced different judgments. We argue that fact-checking becomes politically effective when the meaning of a claim is preserved, the correction reaches the people discussing it, and the source of the correction is recognized as credible. This explains why an accurate fact-check can still have limited public influence.

previous_week_catch_up.title: A dual-attribution framework reveals how foreign investment and trade redistribute cobalt availability
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Global resource allocation is increasingly shaped by foreign direct investment (FDI) and international trade, yet their combined effects on distribution of critical mineral availability across countries remain poorly quantified. Here, we develop a dual-attribution framework covering 193 countries and 36 territories that attributes primary cobalt availability according to corporate ownership and secondary availability according to international trade. We compare these estimates with a combined baseline scenario using geographic-production and pre-trade perspectives to assess how ownership and trade reshape country-level cobalt availability. Relative to this baseline, total cobalt availability is higher in 63.6% of countries, while 72.7% show a positive composite change when primary and secondary availability are equally weighted. Although these mechanisms do not alter the global total amount of cobalt available, they reduce its concentration across countries. Our findings highlight how FDI and trade reshape cobalt distribution and support resource-governance policies that account for both host and exporting countries. This study shows how foreign investment and international trade reshape global cobalt availability. A dual-attribution framework reveals higher attributed availability in most countries while reducing country-level concentration.

previous_week_catch_up.title: A self-limiting mechanotransduction feedback loop ensures robust organ formation
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Organ morphogenesis uses mechanotransduction feedback loops to convert forces into gene expression changes that regulate cell mechanics. How these loops integrate with developmental programs to ensure robust outcomes remains unclear. We show Yap mechanotransduction establishes a self-limiting positive feedback loop for semicircular canal formation in zebrafish. Canal development proceeds through bud initiation, extension, and fusion within the otic epithelium. Local swelling of hyaluronan-rich extracellular matrix (ECM) in the bud activates Yap in a spatial pattern. Yap induces its target ccn1l1 , promoting further ECM expansion to sustain bud extension. This feedback loop confers developmental robustness: graded knockdown of ccn1l1 reduces extension rate, yet canal formation persists and fails only with strong disruption. Critically, the loop contains its own termination mechanism. During bud fusion, PKA-CREB signaling, activated by an adhesion GPCR, gpr126, suppresses ccn1l1 , ending the loop. These findings reveal how mechanotransduction loops with built-in termination provide developmental control by integrating mechanical forces, transcriptional responses, and morphogenetic outcomes.

previous_week_catch_up.title: CREST functions as a molecular bridge between neuron-specific enhancers and epigenetic regulators in mature motor neurons
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Motor neuron development requires precise transcriptional regulation mediated in part by BAF (BRG1/BRM-associated factor) chromatin remodeling complexes. The neuron-specific BAF subunit CREST is critical for neuronal function and is mutated in some cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), yet its underlying genomic mechanisms remain unclear. Using mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation, we show that CREST is essential for motor neuron maturation by activating mature neuronal genes and repressing progenitor genes. Mechanistically, CREST interacts with the neuronal transcription factors ONECUT1 and NGN2, and the BRM ATPase to target pre-existing accessible enhancers of neuronal genes. CREST deletion selectively prevents CBP histone acetyltransferase recruitment, reducing histone H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers and downregulating target gene expression, without disrupting BRM binding, enhancer accessibility, or long-range chromatin architecture. Overall, our findings identify CREST as a crucial epigenetic mediator bridging lineage-specific transcription factors, BAF complexes, and CBP to activate enhancers and promote proper motor neuron development.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Extensive genomic diversity in Desulfovibrio reveals species-specific functional traits associated with disease
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Desulfovibrio spp. are associated with inflammatory diseases and human health, yet limited representative genomes and isolates hinder our understanding of their role in disease. Here, we assembled a comprehensive database of 2658 Desulfovibrio genomes across 90 diseases and 32 countries, including 24 human isolates. Genomic analyses showed extensive species diversity and revealed disease-associated functional traits, including flagellin and adaptation-associated genes (i.e., ureases). Flagellin-mediated Toll-like receptor 5 activation was species-specific and D. desulfuricans flagellin downregulated TGF-beta signalling in murine small intestinal organoids, suggesting impaired immune tolerance. Additionally, we investigated genomic capacity for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) production, a main Desulfovibrio metabolite. While health- and disease-associated Desulfovibrio spp. mainly encoded dissimilatory sulfate reduction, tetrathionate metabolism-encoding bacteria were exclusively detected in inflammatory bowel diseases, including Proteus mirabilis and Morganella morganii . Overall, our study provides a comprehensive genomic Desulfovibrio resource and identifies new links associating strain variation, functional traits and H 2 S-production with inflammatory diseases.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography using explicit neural fields
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. However, existing simultaneous fluorescence-phase techniques primarily operate in transmission mode and are limited to thin specimens, restricting their use in thick tissues and in vivo applications. Although multiphoton microscopy enables deep-tissue fluorescence imaging, combining it with three-dimensional refractive-index (RI) imaging remains challenging because few methods can reconstruct the RI of bulky, label-free tissues in reflection mode at subcellular resolution. Here, we introduce fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography (FDT), which reconstructs the 3D RI of label-free and fluorescence-labeled objects from diffracted fluorescence images acquired in reflection mode under two-photon excitation. FDT uses the transport of intensity equation and a self-supervised neural network based on explicit neural fields. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. We demonstrate FDT in two experimental regimes: reconstructing the 3D RI of label-free tissues up to 300 μ m thick placed on a fluorescent substrate, and reconstructing the 3D RI of fluorescence-labeled, 3D-cultured cells without transmission-side access using fluorescence emitted by the cells themselves. FDT establishes a foundation for accessible reflection-mode multimodal fluorescence-phase imaging in complex biological systems.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Giant step-boundary-triggered nonlocal modulation of magnetization reversal in multi-stepped van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Control of magnetization reversal is crucial for spintronic memory and logic devices. Previous studies on two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) magnets have largely treated magnetic regions in isolation, leaving the roles of step boundaries comparatively unexplored. Here, we investigate step-boundary-triggered nonlocal modulation of magnetization reversal in multi-stepped Fe3GaTe2 using Kerr microscopy, Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, and micromagnetic simulations. Our results indicate that step boundaries can serve as preferential sites for premature nucleation, giving rise to two distinct regimes. In Type I, reversal initiated in a thicker region propagates rapidly across the step boundary, reducing the coercivity of an adjacent thinner region by up to 59.3%. In Type II, stripe domains originating from the thicker region progressively enter the thinner region, shifting its critical switching field polarity and transforming its hysteresis loop from square to slanted, accompanied by a transition in the dominant reversal mode from rapid domain-wall motion to stripe domain growth. Similar behavior in Fe3GeTe2 suggests that step-boundary-mediated modulation may occur more broadly in layered van der Waals ferromagnets. Our findings highlight step engineering as a potential non-invasive strategy for designing efficient and thermally stable vdW spintronic devices. Boundaries can serve as nucleation points for magnetic domains, influencing the switching behavior. Here, Chen, Liu, Zhang, Chen and co-authors study magnetization reversal from stepped boundaries in van der Waals magnets, finding two distinct regimes of switching.

previous_week_catch_up.title: H3K27M cooperates with ASCL1 to maintain progenitor states and drive gliomagenesis
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitutions (H3K27M) drive aggressive diffuse midline gliomas by blocking differentiation of radial glial progenitor cells committed to oligodendrogenesis. We establish prolonged differentiation as a powerful tool to uncover regulators of glioma cell states and demonstrate that the pioneer transcription factor (TF) ASCL1 is a key mediator of H3K27M-driven plasticity and tumorigenesis. H3K27M prevents Polycomb silencing of ASCL1 , co-opting this TF to maintain oligodendroglial progenitor states. Consistently, ASCL1 loss drastically impairs tumor formation in vivo. Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. ASCL1 loss acts as a “fire exit”, enabling alternative differentiation despite H3K27M, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting stalled differentiation and tumor plasticity in histone-mutant gliomas and cancers with a stem cell hierarchy.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Intrinsically flexible inorganic piezoelectric subnanowire enables wireless wearable bioelectronics for non-invasive multimodal human-machine interfacing
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Piezoelectric electronic skin (PE-skin) offers a significant advantage in detecting minute forces, making it highly promising for human-computer interaction in health management and medical rehabilitation. However, PE-skin often faces challenges in real-time, wireless transmission of sensing data, which can compromise both data accuracy and user comfort. Here, we report the synthesis of an inorganic piezoelectric polyoxometalate-based subnanowire, ZnBiPMo12, which possesses intrinsic flexibility and chirality, a piezoelectric coefficient of 24.9 pC/N, and notable ferroelectricity. Leveraging its piezoelectric response, ZnBiPMo12-based PE-skin (1) demonstrates high elasticity and sensitivity to tiny pressures in the range of 0.045-0.319 N. Building on this, a wireless, wearable bioelectronic (WBE) device (1A) is fabricated through multi-level assembly, enabling non-invasive, multimodal monitoring of human physiological signals, including subtle muscle contractions, blinking, breathing, and all-day heart rate. By integrating a machine learning system, a 1-based facial-computer interface (1B) can accurately recognize nine emotional expressions and twelve spoken words. This work not only introduces a typical inorganic piezoelectric material with intrinsic flexibility but also demonstrates scalable manufacturing from subnanomaterials to wireless WBEs, paving the way for non-invasive, multimodal monitoring of human physiological signals and advanced human-computer interaction. Piezoelectric materials enable bioelectronic sensing by converting mechanical stimuli into electrical signals. Xu et al. introduce intrinsically flexible polyoxometalate-based subnanowires and demonstrate their scalable integration into wireless wearable systems for human physiological monitoring.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Nitrous acid (HONO) is a crucial urban source of HOx radicals, promoting surface ozone (O3) and secondary fine particle (PM2.5) formation, yet its long-term evolution and air-quality impacts remain poorly constrained. Here, using a deep neural network established on worldwide field campaigns, we reconstruct global surface HONO distributions. Typical megacities exhibited contrasting trends in 2005–2021, marked by a sharp decline in Beijing (−47.4% in 2013–2021), an increase in Delhi (+10.0% in 2005–2018), and slight decreases in London, New York and Los Angeles. These HONO changes are identified as major driver of O3 and particulate nitrate variations, outweighing contributions of conventional NOx and volatile organic compounds abatement in Beijing and Delhi, while showing comparable impacts in the remaining cities. A fused data-driven framework further uncovers regime-dependent HONO reduction strategies, prioritizing NOx control in summer and co-reduction of NOx, PM2.5 and direct combustion emissions in winter, to accelerate O3 and PM2.5 joint mitigation. Deep learning reveals a sharp decline of HONO in China, modest drops in EU and US but an increase in India. HONO changes drive O3 and PM2.5 variations, outweighing traditional NOx and VOC control, calling for HONO-targeted air quality management.

previous_week_catch_up.title: PRPF19 drives hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis via PKM2-mediated glycolytic reprogramming
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) is a pivotal event driving fibrogenic remodeling of the injured liver. However, the upstream regulators that integrate post-translational signaling with metabolic reprogramming during HSC activation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify pre-mRNA processing factor 19 (PRPF19) as a ubiquitination-linked metabolic regulator that promotes HSC activation. PRPF19 expression was elevated in human and murine fibrotic livers, enriched in activated HSCs, and positively correlated with fibrosis severity. Conditional deletion of Prpf19 in HSCs (Prpf19flox/flox;Lrat-CreERT2), but not in hepatocytes (Prpf19flox/flox;Alb-CreERT2), attenuated HSC activation and liver fibrosis in vivo. Integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses indicated that PRPF19 sustains glycolytic flux and transcriptional programs associated with HSC activation. Mechanistically, PRPF19 promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), facilitating its nuclear translocation and hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α)-dependent transcription of glycolytic and fibrogenic genes. These findings support a role for the PRPF19-PKM2 pathway in metabolic regulation during HSC activation and liver fibrosis. Zhang et al. show that PRPF19 promotes hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis by driving PKM2-dependent glycolytic reprogramming, identifying a potential metabolic target in chronic liver disease.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Direct monitoring the multifaceted intracellular microenvironment is fundamental for deciphering localized cellular behavior and function. However, performing nanoscale spatiotemporal sensing of the dynamic physiochemical environment within a live cell has remained challenging, mainly limited by the lack of robust, biocompatible method which satisfies the requirements for spatiotemporal resolution, sensitivity, multi-physical sensing capability and long-term viability. Here we present a super-resolution-based quantum biosensing approach, namely Super-resolution Multi-physical field Imaging with Deconvolution, implemented in our custom-built setup which integrates nitrogen vacancy center-based quantum sensing with structured illumination microscopy. This enables quantitative, super-resolved, and long-term tracking of intracellular physical fields, featuring spatial resolution of 136 nm, temporal resolution of 150 ms, and field of view of 180×180 μm2. We further perform super-resolution multimodal imaging in a live cell, revealing the spatially heterogeneous reactive oxygen species dynamics under external stimulation. Our work enables the dynamic assessment of localized physiochemical dynamics under super-resolution quantum biosensing. This work presents a super-resolution quantum biosensing approach by integrating nitrogen vacancy (NV) center-based quantum nanodiamond sensors with structured illumination microscopy, which achieves super-resolution multi-physical imaging within live cells.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Somatosensory cortex shapes perceptual decision bias via the superior colliculus
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Sensory inputs reach cortical and subcortical areas in parallel, but how they coordinate to guide decisions remains unknown. We examined the roles of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the superior colliculus (SC) in mice performing whisker-mediated tactile detection. While inactivating S1 contralateral to the stimulus increased detection threshold, inactivating ipsilateral S1 decreased it. These opposing effects reflected shifts in choice bias rather than sensitivity. Unilateral SC inactivation produced similar directional effects, whereas bilateral inactivation of either S1 or SC neutralized bias. Furthermore, SC lesions impaired detection performance, and combined S1 inactivation caused no further impairment, indicating that S1-mediated shifts in bias were SC-dependent. S1 inactivation also decreased sensory-evoked neural activity in SC, and choice decoding revealed that behavioral impairment was more closely associated with changes in SC population activity than with loss of sensory encoding in S1. Thus, S1 shapes perceptual bias by modulating SC-dependent circuits that transform sensory evidence into perceptual decisions.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Structural basis of ammonium transport and coordinated regulation of AMT1;1 in Arabidopsis thaliana
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract Efficient ammonium uptake is essential for plant growth and nitrogen-use efficiency, yet the structural basis of ammonium transport and regulation in plant AMTs remains unclear. Here, we determined multiple cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Arabidopsis thaliana ammonium transporter AMT1;1 in apo, ammonium-bound, methylammonium-bound, low-pH and phosphomimetic states. These structures reveal a conserved ammonium conduction pathway comprising an aromatic recruitment vestibule, a Phe-gate/Twin-His-containing pore, and a polar intracellular exit region. We further identified a conserved extracellular N-terminal disulfide bond required for oligomer stability and transport activity, suggesting potential redox-dependent regulation. On the cytoplasmic side, phosphorylation modulates C-terminal interactions with intracellular loops, revealing an allosteric regulatory mechanism. Comparison with the bacterial ammonium-sensing protein Sd -Amt1 uncovers a conserved ammonium-recognition region in At AMT1;1 that contributes to transport activity but lacks the signaling module and ligand-dependent conformational switching observed in Sd -Amt1. Together, these findings provide structural insight into ammonium transport and coordinated regulation in plant AMT transporters.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Transposable element-mediated structural variations shape gene expression and agronomic trait diversity in Brassica napus
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Brassica napus is a globally important allotetraploid oilseed crop with a complex genome and extensive structural diversity that remains incompletely characterized. Here, we present gap-free reference genome assemblies for Zhongshuang 11 (ZS11) and Westar, and assemble six additional accessions. We harmonize gene annotations across 22 genomes and develop BnaScope (https://rgmi.hzau.edu.cn/bnascope), a gene-centric functional genomics platform. Gene-based and graph-based pan-genomes identify 123,107 non-redundant gene clusters and 188,218 structural variants, including 112,417 transposable element-mediated structural variants (TEMSVs). TEMSVs show asymmetric distributions between An and Cn subgenomes and are associated with increased homoeolog expression imbalance, particularly for CDS-TEMSVs. SV-based genome-wide association analyses identify candidate genes underlying seed quality traits, and functional analyses demonstrate that BnaPYRDs negatively regulate seed glucosinolate content. These findings establish structural variation as an important contributor to homoeolog regulation and seed-quality variation in B. napus. This study develops a comprehensive pan-genome resource for Brassica napus and reveals how structural variations shape gene regulation and seed quality traits. The findings provide insights into genome diversity and crop improvement.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Twisted superconducting quantum diodes for high fidelity anharmonic qubits
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract In superconducting circuits, bidirectional signal propagation can cause back-reflections and back-action that couple environmental noise back to coherent elements, degrading fidelity. Nonreciprocal superconducting diodes provide an intrinsic route to suppress such back-scattering at the circuit level. However, their diode efficiency and quantum integration remain limited. Here, we realize a quantum diode in twisted NbSe 2 under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields. A mere 1 ∘ twist yields an efficiency enhancement over pristine devices, reaching 27.6%. Quantum simulations reveal that this intermediate efficiency, well below 100% ideal, is both experimentally practical and optimal for preserving qubit anharmonicity and stabilizing two-level systems. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits.

previous_week_catch_up.title: A co-evolved peptide-GPCR system senses host entry to drive fungal infection
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract A successful infection requires pathogens to recognize the specific host environment in order to reprogram their physiology accordingly. One major way in which eukaryotic cells sense their surroundings is via G-Protein Coupled Receptors (GPCRs), which share a seven-transmembrane architecture and G-protein-mediated downstream signaling. While mammalian GPCRs are well-characterized and represent important drug targets, their fungal counterparts remain poorly understood. Here we uncover a GPCR-based mechanism that allows the corn pathogen Ustilago maydis to sense whether it has entered plant tissue. During infection, the fungus secretes the protein Pit2, which is cleaved by host apoplastic cysteine proteases, releasing a peptide ligand ‘hidden’ within the protein core. This ligand activates the fungal GPCR Gpe1, thus promoting fungal proliferation after initial host penetration. We elucidate the crystal structure of Pit2 and model the complex formed by Gpe1 and the Pit2-derived peptide. Structure-guided mutational analysis supports that disrupting this interaction reduces fungal virulence. The Gpe1/Pit2 system is conserved in related fungal species, with co-evolutionary signatures apparently preserving receptor-ligand specificity. Furthermore, this system shows mechanistic similarities to mammalian receptors, suggesting an evolutionary link between fungal and mammalian GPCRs.

previous_week_catch_up.title: ATM promotes nucleolytic processing of reversed replication forks during DNA interstrand cross-link repair
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: During replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) repair, fork reversal is thought to enable the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway to resolve the ICL through nucleolytic incisions. The resulting regressed arm of the reversed fork undergoes extensive nucleolytic resection that may facilitate completion of replication. Despite the importance of these remodeling events, their regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we use cell-free Xenopus egg extracts and human cells to investigate reversed fork processing during ICL repair by the FA pathway. We find that the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase is activated concomitantly with fork reversal and promotes resection of reversed fork intermediates. ATM enhances chromatin recruitment of DNA2, which acts alongside EXO1 to resect reversed forks formed during ICL repair. Moreover, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) leads to ATM hyperactivation, accelerated reversed fork processing, and accumulation of aberrant end-joining products, implying that PP2A restrains ATM signaling to limit reversed fork resection. Taken together, this work identifies reversed forks as substrates for ATM activation and reveals a phospho-regulatory circuit that controls reversed fork processing. Replication stress often induces fork reversal, which protects stalled replication intermediates until replication can resume. This study identifies the ATM kinase as a key regulator that promotes nuclease-dependent processing of reversed fork structures formed at DNA interstrand cross-links.

previous_week_catch_up.title: CROSS: A cross-species chromosome substitution platform for dissecting chromosome architecture and activity
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: The functional integrity of a mammalian chromosome depends on its long-term co-evolution with species-specific nuclear environment. How chromosomes co-adapt with their native environment to define 3D architecture and transcription remains unclear, largely due to a lack of experimental models that dissect this co-evolution. Here, we report cross-species chromosome substitution (CROSS), a method enabling stable, scarless replacement of host chromosomes with divergent orthologs. We integrate microcell-mediated chromosome transfer with CRISPR/Cas9 to import the intact 152-Mb rat X chromosome into male mouse embryonic stem cells, and subsequently replace the mouse X chromosome, maintaining its stability and integrity. Rat-specific LINE1 and RatSatRep2 repeats recruit mouse SETDB1 inefficiently, causing local H3K9me3 loss. This triggers 3D remodeling, characterized by de novo topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries that aberrantly activate adjacent genes, including Rhox5, impairing differentiation. We provide a platform for dissecting sequence and epigenome cooperation in chromosome regulation, and evaluating fidelity of large-scale heterologous DNA. Chromosome function depends on coevolution with nuclear environment, but how is unclear. Here, authors use CROSS to stably and scarlessly replace mouse chrX with rat chrX. Rat repeats poorly recruit SETDB1, causing H3K9me3 loss, new TAD boundaries, that dysregulate genes, impairing differentiation.

previous_week_catch_up.title: De novo design of miniprotein inhibitors of bacterial adhesins
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: The rise of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections necessitates the discovery of novel antimicrobial strategies. Here, we show that protein design provides a generalizable means of generating new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins, which are virulence factors critical in host-pathogen interactions. We de novo designed high-affinity miniprotein binders to FimH and Abp chaperone usher pili adhesins from uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii, respectively, which are implicated in mediating both uncomplicated and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI) responsible for significant morbidity worldwide. The designed antagonists have high specificity and stability, disrupt bacterial recognition of host receptors, block biofilm formation, and are effective in treating and preventing murine models of uncomplicated and catheter-associated UTIs in vivo. Here, the authors show that protein design is a generalizable strategy to generate new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins to combat two causative agents of urinary tract infections, E. coli and A. baumannii.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Environmentally Relevant Concentrations of Nanomaterials Drive Photochemical Production of Reactive Species and Pollutant Degradation in Surface Waters
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Reactive intermediates in surface waters are widely attributed to dissolved organic matter (DOM). Natural, incidental, or engineered nanomaterials simultaneously occur at parts per billion and can function as photocatalysts, yet the photochemical role of nanomaterials at environmentally relevant concentrations remains overlooked in surface water photochemistry. Here, we quantify reactive intermediates from TiO2 nanomaterials (1–100 μg L−1) and DOM (1–5 mgC L−1) under 222, 265, and 365 nm. Despite lower concentrations relative to DOM, TiO2 produces hydroxyl radical (HO•) rates 10× to 100× higher per unit mass, resulting in comparable HO• formation. DOM plus nanomaterial mixtures shows synergistic behavior, with HO• formation 16-21% above additive predictions. DOM has limited impact in the degradation of 6PPD-quinone whereas nanomaterials enhanced its degradation due to elevated [HO•]ss. These results demonstrate nanomaterials can contribute to or exceed DOM in HO• driven micropollutant degradation in surface waters or engineered ultraviolet-light water treatment systems. Environmentally relevant nanomaterial concentrations can rival dissolved organic matter in driving pollutant transformation under sunlight or UV-based water treatment.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Fast-charging and durable all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries enabled by pre-embedded solid-solid redox mediator
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: All-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries promise high specific energy and low cost. However, they are challenged by poor rate capability and cycling stability owing to the slow solid-solid sulfur redox reactions. Here, we present fast-charging and durable all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries enabled by a pre-embedded solid-solid redox mediator using an amorphous sulfur/iodine nano-eutectic positive electrode. The iodine, intimately homogenized with sulfur owing to carbon mesopore encapsulation, undergoes rapid I2/I− redox reaction, mediating solid-solid sulfur reactions by promoting electron transfer across the boundaries. The iodine within the carbon and on its surface reacts in situ with the sulfide catholyte to form a globally distributed I2/I− nano-network throughout the positive electrode, thereby enabling fast charging. The cell exhibits a specific capacity of 851.9 mA h g−1S/I when charged at 10 C, and 474.7 mA h g−1S/I at a charging rate of 24 C (1 C is defined as 945 mA g−1S/I). The high reversibility of the redox-mediated reaction enables durable cycling for 9,000 cycles over 9 months at 2 C and 2,800 cycles over 17 months at 0.5 C. This strategy represents a perspective for developing solid-state conversion electrodes that are plagued by sluggish reactions. All-solid-state lithium sulfur batteries suffer from sluggish solid-solid sulfur redox reactions. Here, the authors report fast charging and durable all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries enabled by a pre-embedded solid-solid redox mediator in an amorphous sulfur/iodine nano-eutectic positive electrode.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Freezing-induced solid-liquid microphase separation for self-assembly of functional nucleic acid nanoparticles
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: In nature, nuclear DNA complexed with histone form highly condensed chromatin via loop extrusion and microphase separation, yielding physically constrained solid-like structures. Inspired by this natural compaction, here we demonstrate that freezing-induced crystallization pressure and freeze-concentration effects trigger solid-liquid microphase separation for efficient DNA compression. Freezing compress various nucleic acids (single stranded DNA, molecular beacons, siRNA, plasmid DNA) into high-density states that self-assemble into nanoparticles (DNA-NPs, MB-NPs, siBcl-2-NPs, siPLK1-NPs, pEGFP-NPs). Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that ice crystal growth increases solute concentration, enhancing DNA intermolecular interactions to form supramolecular chains. Stress at advancing ice-liquid interfaces further orders and compacts these supramolecular chains into nanoparticles. In breast cancer cells, MB-NPs detect miRNA-21; siBcl-2-NPs downregulate Bcl-2 protein; siPLK1-NPs exhibited antitumor effects; and pEGFP-NPs mediate green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression. This freeze-induced self-assembly strategy replaces chemical synthesis with physical constraints, establishing a versatile platform for facile production of nucleic acid nanoparticles. Efficent delivery of various nucleic acids in vitro and in vivo remains challenging. Here, the authors use freezing-induced condensation and microphase separation to compress nucleic acids into functional nanoparticles, without excipients, validated the bioactivity in vitro and in vivo.

previous_week_catch_up.title: FtmOx1-catalyzed diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization enables versatile late-stage diversification of phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: The enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds has emerged as a transformative strategy in medicinal chemistry. Verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is known to catalyze the endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, we demonstrate the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 by showing its ability to mediate diverse C(sp3)-H transformations on non-native substrates—phenethylamine and tetrahydroisoquinoline derivatives (1) —including β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α,β-desaturation. A total of 48 structurally diverse substrates prove suitable for this method, substantially expanding the biocatalytic repertoire of FtmOx1. Mechanistic studies, combined with crystallographic and mutagenesis analyses, reveal the distinct molecular basis for this diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization compared to native pathway. Notably, the relative flexibility of the phenethyl and benzyl chains of 1, assisted by specific substitutions that allow the two chains to swing, enables high β-selectivity for hydroxylation and prevents secondary oxidation. This C(sp3)-H activation platform efficiently generates structurally diverse oxyfunctionalized derivatives, including 1,2-amino alcohols (2), 1,2-amino ketones (3), and enamines (4), accelerating lead discovery for modulators of the human relaxin family peptide receptor 4 (RXFP4). Collectively, our work establishes FtmOx1 as a powerful biocatalytic tool, expanding the frontiers of C–H functionalization in drug discovery. Enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds is an important strategy in medicinal chemistry, and verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is an enzyme that catalyses endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, the authors report the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 in mediating diverse C(sp3)-H transformations of non-native substrates, including phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines, through β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α, β-desaturation.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Lipid-organized tetramerization of PLPP1 defines the molecular basis of spatial lipid phosphate signaling
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Bioactive lipid phosphates, such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and sphingosine-1-phosphate, are potent membrane-embedded signals that regulate fundamental processes in development, immunity, and cancer. The termination of these signals is mediated by phospholipid phosphatases (PLPPs), yet the molecular principles governing their function at the membrane interface have remained poorly understood. Here we report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of human PLPP1 in apo (1.87 Å) and product-bound (2.21 Å) states. The structures reveal a highly ordered, C4-symmetric homotetramer with ordered lipid densities—including densities assigned to phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidic acid, and phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate—at inter-subunit interfaces. Structure-guided mutagenesis shows that residues surrounding these interfacial lipid densities affect enzymatic activity, whereas oligomerization analysis indicates that activity loss does not simply correlate with tetramer disruption. The product-bound structure defines the catalytic pocket and a membrane-facing tunnel that suggests a possible route for LPA access, while electrophysiological recordings detected no PLPP1-associated ion conductance under the conditions tested. Together, these findings provide a structural framework for PLPP1 tetramer assembly, lipid phosphate hydrolysis, and product recognition. Lipid phosphate phosphatases regulate bioactive lipids involved in cell signalling. Here, the authors reveal how human PLPP1 assembles and recognizes lipids, providing a structural framework for its membrane-associated activity.

previous_week_catch_up.title: MACF1 condensates serve as molecular rheostats translating mechanical stress into bone adaptation
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Bone dynamically maintains homeostasis through mechanotransduction, a process essential for skeletal integrity and frequently disrupted in disease. Yet how bone cells decode mechanical cues into adaptive responses remains poorly understood. Here, we identify MACF1, a cytoskeletal crosslinker and core component of stress granules (SGs), as a mechanosensitive scaffold that undergoes phase separation via its intrinsically disordered region 2 (IDR2). In response to distinct mechanical cues, IDR2-driven condensation promotes the recruitment of PIEZO1, paxillin (PXN), and β-catenin (CTNNB1) into SGs, buffering these signaling molecules from ubiquitination-dependent degradation and sustaining osteogenic fidelity. Moreover, we identify an arginine-mutated IDR2 variant that separates protein interactions from condensate formation, revealing IDR2-driven phase separation as a requirement for MACF1-mediated SG assembly and mechanosensitive protein recruitment. Functionally, bone-targeted delivery of MACF1-IDR2 alleviates mechanical unloading-induced bone loss in male mice. These findings reveal a liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)-mediated mechanism linking mechanical force sensing and transduction to bone adaptation. Together, these findings support a model in which MACF1 condensates act as molecular rheostats that coordinate mechano-responsive cargo sorting under stress and contribute to skeletal homeostasis. The authors show that mechanosensitive phase separation of MACF1 promotes stress granule formation and mechanosensitive protein recruitment, limiting their ubiquitin-mediated degradation. This supports bone mechanotransduction and homeostasis.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Periodontal pathogen Tannerella forsythia promotes liver fibrosis via ICAM-1⁺ neutrophil–dependent hepatic stellate cell activation
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Periodontitis is a key driver in the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Nevertheless, how specific periodontal pathogens contribute to liver fibrosis remains elusive. Here, we identify Tannerella forsythia as the crucial mediator in the link between periodontitis and liver fibrosis, which can translocate to the gut and aggravate liver fibrosis. Mechanistically, Tannerella forsythia promotes the infiltration of ICAM-1+ neutrophils and inflammatory response in the liver via disrupting intestinal barrier integrity. ICAM-1+ neutrophils secrete TNF-α, which activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in hepatic stellate cells, triggering collagen deposition and fibrogenesis. Conditional knockout of ICAM-1 in neutrophils or global deletion of TNF-α significantly attenuates inflammatory response and liver fibrosis caused by Tannerella forsythia. Taken together, this study identifies an oral-gut-liver axis driven by Tannerella forsythia and provides a prospective therapeutic target for periodontitis-related liver fibrosis. Peridontitis has been linked in the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Here the authors suggest that Tannerella forsythia is linked to the promotion of liver fibrosis by ICAM-1+ neutrophils activating hepatic stellate cells.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Recognition and mechanism of M. tuberculosis cell wall galactan transport
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Mycobacterial-derived lipid-linked galactan (LLG) is an essential component of the Mycobacterial tuberculosis (Mtb) cell wall core arabinogalactan (AG), a well-established virulence factor and target of anti-tubercular drugs. Cross-membrane translocation of LLG is energetically unfavorable and is therefore catalyzed by WzmWzt, a prominent member of the polysaccharide ABC transporter sub-family. Here we present cryo-EM structures of WzmWztMtb to uncover critical steps of Mtb LLG translocation. Notably, densities suggestive of the mycobacterial-derived LLG substrates were observed in the structure of WzmWztMtb, indicating that the substrate may bind through two Wzm and two Wzt subunits. This proposed LLG binding is fulfilled by a fully upward extension of the Wzt gate helix, which serves as a critical step to prime Wzt for dimerization. The ATP-bound structure revealed a remarkable downward movement of the gate helix, together with the Wzt dimerization. The third, DDM/ATP-bound structure captured WztWzmMtb in an intermediate state with two DDM molecules in the Wzm central cavity. Using two conditional mycobacterial mutants for functional analyses, we have identified residues on the Wzm N-terminal interface helix (IFN) and on the Wzt helical domain are essential for LLG recognition and translocation in vivo. These data provide a clear structural basis for the development of Mtb cell wall targeted therapeutics for global tuberculosis treatment. In this work, Wei and colleagues reveal how an essential Mycobacterium tuberculosis transporter recognizes and translocates a cell-wall galactan chain across the membrane, providing a structural framework for developing tuberculosis drugs.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Resistance indicators in sewage microbiota mirror clinical antibiotic use with temporal lag linked to host
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Wastewater-based surveillance (WBS) offers a promising window into community pathogens but extending it to antibiotic resistance (AR) is complicated by ecological and physical processes within sewer systems. The epidemiological meaning of antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) abundances in sewage remains unclear because signals reflect both human-derived inputs and in-sewer microbial dynamics. Using a unique 5-year dataset of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions and a yearlong, twice-weekly metagenomic survey of a single wastewater treatment plant, we differentiate associations between sewage-borne antibiotic-resistant bacteria and community antibiotic use. We find that ARGs linked to Enterobacteriaceae track closely with antibiotic usage, while those associated with ecologically-distinct Pseudomonadaceae show lagged correlations of 1–3 months. Nested statistical modeling further links Pseudomonas MAG dynamics with lagged sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim use after accounting for sewage characteristics and seasonality. Our results demonstrate that WBS can capture local patterns of epidemiologically relevant AR when microbial ecological factors shaping sewage signals are considered. Profiles of antibiotic resistance genes in wastewater still often lack epidemiological context. In this study, the authors use wastewater metagenomics and antibiotic use data to reveal a variable lagging association between human antibiotic consumption and antibiotic resistance genes in sewage-derived bacterial hosts.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Single-cell atlas of fetal immunity across lung, spleen, and umbilical cord blood in nonhuman primates
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: The fetal immune system develops within a tightly regulated environment that balances immune tolerance with readiness for postnatal antigen exposure. However, limited fetal tissue access constrains understanding of immune ontogeny across compartments. Here we present a multi-tissue single-cell transcriptional atlas of the late-gestation (GD130-135) rhesus macaque fetal immune system, profiling leukocytes from lung, spleen, and umbilical cord blood (UCBMC) spanning myeloid, lymphoid, innate lymphoid, and hematopoietic stem cell lineages. Fetal lung is enriched in myeloid cells and ILC2s and shows a proinflammatory bias. Spleen is dominated by T and B cells, with B cells showing enhanced signatures of V(D)J recombination and isotype switching and CD4 T cells showing increased activation and Treg frequency. UCBMC is predominantly composed of T cells with a regulatory transcriptional landscape. Spectral flow cytometry and functional assays corroborate these tissue-specific differences revealing elevated secretion of inflammatory mediators in fetal lung at rest, while spleen and UCBMC show greater inducible responses following stimulation. Together, these data provide a comprehensive cross-tissue atlas of late-gestation primate fetal immunity, revealing tissue-specific immune specialization, functional capacity, and intercellular communication networks that shape immune readiness prior to birth. Investigations into fetal immune ontogeny across compartments are constrained by tissue inaccessibility during pregnancy. This rhesus macaque single-cell atlas profiles fetal lung, spleen, and cord blood, revealing tissue specific immune cell composition and activation at late-gestation validated by flow cytometry and functional assays.

previous_week_catch_up.title: The conformation-selective PI3Kδ inhibitor roginolisib in patients with advanced or metastatic cancer, including metastatic uveal melanoma: first-in-human clinical trial
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase delta (PI3Kδ) promotes tumour cell growth directly or indirectly by activating immune-suppressive cells. In contrast to previous PI3Kδ inhibitors, roginolisib is a selective, non-ATP competitive inhibitor, which locks PI3Kδ into an inactive state and causes an allosteric modulation. In a First-in-Human dose study, continuous daily dosing of roginolisib was investigated in patients with solid and haematologic malignancies. In Part A, 24 patients received escalating doses of roginolisib. In Part B, 20 mostly pre-treated metastatic uveal melanoma (mUM) patients received a dose associated with continuous PI3Kδ inhibition of >90%. The primary endpoint was safety, and secondary endpoints included pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) profile, clinical anti-tumour responses assessments. Exploratory endpoints included immunophenotyping, proteomics, genomics. No Dose Limiting Toxicity or drug related toxicities requiring dose modifications were observed ( ≥ Grade 3 toxicities: 3/44; 6.8%). In mUM, median Overall Survival (mOS) was 20.8 months (data-cut off December 2023) and 18.4 months (data-cut-off February 2026). mOS in mUM patients with Stable Disease at Week 16 ( = Cycle 5) was 28.5 months, while patients who progressed at Week 16 had a median OS of 12.3 months. Roginolisib was safe, had a predictable PK profile, T regulatory cell abundance was decreased while activated CD8+ T cells increased together with soluble plasma IL-15. ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT04328844. First generation inhibitors of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase delta (PI3Kδ) had limited selectivity due to the conserved ATP binding pocket, resulting in toxicity when used as anti-cancer agent. Here, the authors report the results of a first-in-human clinical trial of Roginolisib, a next generation conformation-selective PI3Kδ inhibitor, in patients with advanced or metastatic cancer with dose expansion in patients with metastatic uveal melanoma.

previous_week_catch_up.title: Advancing chemical reaction prediction in data-scarce drug discovery with active and geometric deep learning
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Abstract The success of generative molecular design depends on the synthetic accessibility of the molecules it creates. While computational models can help predict chemical reactions, their current effectiveness is limited by a lack of reference data and the difficulty of accurately predicting reaction regioselectivity. Here, to address this, we present an integrated closed-loop workflow that combines efficient reaction data acquisition with high-accuracy deep learning. We developed an active learning strategy, driven by a tree-based ensemble, to guide the acquisition of the most informative laboratory experiments. This experimental campaign yielded a diverse benchmark for C–H borylation. The bespoke dataset allowed us to train and evaluate geometric graph neural networks. We demonstrate that augmenting these symmetry-aware models with self-supervised auxiliary tasks consistently improves performance for both reaction outcome prediction and regioselectivity prediction. Prospective tests on unseen substrates, featuring challenging N -heteroaryl motifs, pinpointed the correct borylation positions in all cases, illustrating the practical utility of our workflow for efficient drug optimization.

previous_week_catch_up.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
previous_week_catch_up.title: A second-generation “hypoxia in a pill” rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes across distinct mouse models
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: A growing body of preclinical research is demonstrating the therapeutic potential of chronic, continuous hypoxia (11% FIO 2 ) for rare and common diseases. However, the chronic delivery of hypoxic gas poses both practical challenges and long-term safety concerns. We previously introduced a small-molecule, “hypoxia-in-a-pill” combining a hemoglobin affinity enhancer (GBT440) to limit oxygen delivery with a HIF-2α inhibitor (PT2399) to prevent detrimental compensatory erythropoiesis. Although this small-molecule regimen extended the lifespan of the Ndufs4 knockout (KO) mouse model of mitochondrial complex I deficiency and Leigh syndrome, its efficacy did not match chronic 11% FIO 2 . Here we optimize this regimen using GBT601, a second-generation hemoglobin affinity enhancer with longer half-life and greater hemoglobin occupancy, and show it rescues key neurodegenerative phenotypes in multiple models. When we initiate therapy in 50 d old Ndufs4 KO mice with advanced disease, GBT601 monotherapy alleviated neurological disease phenotypes and extended median lifespan from 62 to 105 d, while dual therapy with the GBT601/PT2399 combination extended median lifespan to 158 d. When initiated after onset of advanced disease in a mouse model of Friedreich’s ataxia, the combination halted further progression of motor phenotypes. In a mouse model of Parkinson’s disease due to α-synuclein toxicity, initiating the GBT601/PT2399 combination after onset of motor dysfunction attenuates brain hyperoxia and lipid peroxidation and reverses motor phenotypes. Importantly, the combination maintained body weight without inducing any signs of pulmonary hypertension. Our findings motivate further preclinical and clinical evaluation of our “hypoxia in a pill” approach for diseases with high unmet need.

previous_week_catch_up.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
previous_week_catch_up.title: GTP orchestrates CTP synthase via an allosteric effector–cycling mechanism
previous_week_catch_up.abstract: Cytidine triphosphate (CTP), a fundamental building block of RNA, plays vital roles in diverse biological processes. CTP synthase (CTPS) is the only known enzyme for de novo synthesis of CTP. Efficient CTPS catalysis requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) in a dose-dependent, nonconsumptive manner; however, the precise mechanism by which GTP drives CTP formation remains unclear. Here, we integrate a series of cryo-EM structures of Drosophila melanogaster CTPS captured from actively catalyzing samples with biochemical and mutagenesis analyses, yielding 34 distinct CTPS states at resolutions up to 2.0 Å. We find that GTP binds to and dissociates from CTPS once per catalytic cycle, thereby enabling the production of a single CTP molecule. Initial GTP engagement requires formation of 4-phosphoryl-UTP in the AL domain, whereas full stabilization of GTP binding is promoted by occupancy of the GAT active site. Together, these two checkpoints couple GTP recruitment and stabilization to catalytic progress in the two domains, enabling the coordinated synthesis of one CTP molecule per GTP binding–dissociation cycle. Moreover, the GTP-recognition site is highly conserved across the three domains of life. These findings establish a comprehensive mechanistic framework for efficient CTPS catalysis and define “effector-cycling”—in which GTP undergoes obligatory binding and dissociation during each catalytic cycle to regulate an intermediate step in a multistep catalytic process—as a distinct mode of allosteric regulation.
